NORTH CAROLINA INDUSTRIAL COMMISSION

I.C. NO.

22-030317

,

scott reed

, Employee, Plaintiff v.

the laramar group

,

gallagher bassett services, inc.

Administrator), Defendant.

OPINION AND AWARD for the Full Commission by JAMES C. GILLEN, Commissioner.

Filed: 14 August 2024

This case was heard before the Full Commission on 5 March 2024, upon appeal of

Defendants from an Opinion and Award filed by Deputy Commissioner Wes Saunders on 29

September 2023. The deposition transcript of Dr. Matthew Crawford is part of the evidence of

record.

A P P E A R A N C E S

Plaintiff: Younce, Vtipil, Baznik & Banks; Raleigh, North Carolina;

Robert C. Younce, Jr, appearing.

Defendant: McAngus Goudelock & Courie, PLLC; Raleigh, North Carolina;

Reghan Schmidt, appearing and Carolyn T. Marcus, Counsel of Record.

1

* * * * * * * * * * *

The Full Commission has reviewed the prior Opinion and Award based upon the record

of the proceedings before Deputy Commissioner Saunders, the Form 44

Application for Review

,

and the briefs and arguments of the parties. The Full Commission hereby enters the following

Opinion and Award pursuant to N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-85:

* * * * * * * * * * *

The Full Commission finds as fact and concludes as matters of law the following, which

were entered into by the parties in the executed Pre-Trial Agreement as:

STIPULATIONS

1

On 18 January 2024, Carolyn Marcus filed correspondence with the Industrial Commission stating that she is “no

longer with HPL+P Law” and is “currently with McAngus Goudelock & Courie and I will continue as attorney of

record on [this] file.” As such, Carolyn Marcus, with McAngus, Goudelock & Courie is the attorney of record in

this matter.

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 2

1.

All parties are properly before the Commission, and the Commission has

jurisdiction of the parties and the subject matter.

2.

Plaintiff is Scott A. Reed.

3.

Defendant-Employer is The Laramar Group.

4.

The Third-Party Administrator is Gallagher Bassett Services, Inc.

5.

Defendant-Employer regularly employs three or more employees and is bound by

the North Carolina Workers’ Compensation Act. An employment relationship existed between

Defendant-Employer and Plaintiff on 20 May 2022, the date of alleged injury.

* * * * * * * * * * *

EXHIBITS

The following documents were accepted into evidence by the Deputy Commissioner as

Stipulated Exhibits:

a.

Stipulated Exhibit #1: Executed Pre-Trial Agreement; and

b.

Stipulated Exhibit #2: Indexed set of paginated exhibits including medical records,

Industrial Commission forms and filings, Plaintiff’s personnel file, and Form W-2s from

Food Lion.

* * * * * * * * * * *

The Full Commission addresses the following:

ISSUE

Whether Plaintiff suffered a compensable injury by accident on 20 May 2022, and if so,

to what compensation is Plaintiff entitled?

* * * * * * * * * * *

Based upon a preponderance of the evidence in view of the entire record, and reasonable

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 3

inferences flowing therefrom, the Full Commission makes the following:

FINDINGS OF FACT

1.

Plaintiff, who was 63 years old at the time of the hearing before the Deputy

Commissioner, was hired by Defendant-Employer on 21 February 2022 as a Maintenance

Technician for an apartment complex. Prior to being hired by Defendant-Employer, Plaintiff had

no prior issues with his right shoulder and had no history of injuries or treatment to his right

shoulder.

2.

Plaintiff did not complete high school but achieved a GED when he was a

teenager. Plaintiff has no active professional certifications. Prior to working for Defendant-

Employer, Plaintiff worked various jobs performing mostly maintenance and remodeling

construction work. Plaintiff has experience welding, performing carpentry, installing and

repairing sheet rock, and performing plumbing and electrical work.

3.

Plaintiff’s job duties with Defendant-Employer required him to perform a wide

range of maintenance work. The tasks he was required to perform included, but were not limited

to, changing air filters, unclogging drains, changing HVAC filters, replacing and repairing hot

water heaters, fixing and replacing overhead light fixtures, painting, and performing carpet patch

work.

4.

Defendant-Employer’s Maintenance Technician job description reflects a

requirement “to lift over 50 lbs. consistently throughout an 8-12 hour workday.” Plaintiff

testified that the position required him to lift items weighing over 50 pounds and up to 100

pounds by himself, including stacked washer-dryers, water heaters, bags of garbage, and

furniture. Additionally, Plaintiff explained that his tool bag, which he characterized as

“essentially a duffel bag,” weighs “60 pounds or maybe better, [it] just depends on what all I

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 4

have in it.” Plaintiff customarily carried in his tool bag adjustable wrenches, hammers,

screwdrivers, drill bits, hand tools, batteries, a keyhole saw, rolls of drywall tape, and other tools

and hardware.

5.

On Friday, 20 May 2022, Plaintiff was working in a unit within Building S of the

complex removing kitchen cabinet doors. After finishing this project, at approximately noon, he

loaded his tools into his tool bag, which weighed approximately 60 to 70 pounds at the time, and

walked to his motorized “gator” utility vehicle, which was parked on a steep incline outside

Building S. Plaintiff testified that the ground in this area is sloped at an angle nearing 45

degrees.

6.

The bed of the gator vehicle has wall rails that reach a height of four feet above

level ground. Normally, when lifting an item into the bed of the gator, Plaintiff used two hands

to lift the item up and over its sides. However, Plaintiff credibly testified that, on this occasion,

due to the incline, Plaintiff was unable to maintain his balance while lifting his tool bag with two

hands and therefore “had to swing” the bag in his right hand in order to “get the momentum

going to get over the wall rails” while he held onto the gator’s roll bar with his left hand. On 20

May 2022, while swinging the tool bag over the side of the gator bed’s siderail, Plaintiff felt a

sudden pop in his right shoulder.

7.

The area outside Building S was the only location on the apartment complex’s

grounds that does not have level ground. Plaintiff credibly testified that, except for the occasion

on 20 May 2022, he did not recall, during his employment with Defendant-Employer, ever lifting

his tool bag or any other heavy item into the gator using the method he used on that day.

8.

Plaintiff testified that, in addition to experiencing the pop in his right shoulder,

Plaintiff felt “a sharp pain” which “ran all the way down my arm and into my fingers” as well as

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 5

a “grinding,” “bone on bone” sensation in his right shoulder.

9.

After his injury, Plaintiff drove the gator to the apartment complex office and

reported to his supervisor, Alex Stephenson, that he had “popped” his shoulder.

10.

At that time, Plaintiff still planned to continue working his shift. Because it was

time for Plaintiff’s lunch break, after speaking to Mr. Stephenson Plaintiff traveled to a nearby

Food Lion for a sandwich. Plaintiff testified: “I went over to the grocery store at lunch time, got

me a sandwich from the deli, bought a twelve pack of beer for later, and just by habit reached

over and picked the twelve pack up with my right hand and it popped again.” Plaintiff later

added more detail regarding the beer-lifting incident, testifying: “My shoulder was getting

steadily worse and the . . . pop at the Food Lion, I was able to drop the bag immediately onto the

conveyor belt so, you know, I didn’t hurt myself further.”

11.

Plaintiff departed the Food Lion and returned to the apartment complex office,

having resolved to take the afternoon off to rest due to the injury. Once there, he asked Mr.

Stephenson to load Plaintiff’s tool bag into his car. At that time Mr. Stephenson asked Plaintiff

if he needed to go to the doctor. Plaintiff responded to the effect that he did not know yet, and

that he would evaluate that possibility during the workweek following the weekend.

12.

During the ensuing weekend, Plaintiff’s right shoulder continued to have a steady

and uncomfortable pain. Plaintiff testified that his pain was “bad” and that “it just stayed

throbbing, grinding.”

13.

Plaintiff worked for Defendant-Employer on Monday and Tuesday, 23-24 May

2022.

14.

On Wednesday 25 May 2022, Plaintiff presented to his primary care provider,

Family Nurse Practitioner Nicole Brown, for an evaluation of his right shoulder. The record

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 6

from this visit reflects that Plaintiff reported:

‘2 large pops and grinding and extreme’ [pain] 5 days ago while

picking up his tool bag. Then again same day within 1 hour he

lifted his shopping bag and felt another pop again with extreme

pain. No previous injury to the shoulder . . . Feels some shooting

pain from wrist radiating up, and feels numbness on the ‘ball of my

shoulder.’

On examination of Plaintiff’s right shoulder, Family Nurse Practitioner Brown noted

“Movements are restricted with passive elevation. Movements are painful with flexion,

extension, abduction and adduction. 4/5 strength with rotator cuff testing and hand grip on R.”

Family Nurse Practitioner Brown’s 25 May 2022 record reflects a diagnosis of “Other specified

disorders of tendon, right shoulder—acute” as well as her prescription of prednisone and flexeril.

She referred Plaintiff to EmergeOrtho for further evaluation.

15.

Plaintiff was terminated from his employment with Defendant-Employer

approximately three months after the 20 May 2022 incident. The last day Plaintiff worked for

Defendant-Employer was 6 June 2022. However, based on the Form 22 stipulated into evidence,

it appears Plaintiff was paid his full salary through 10 June 2022.

16.

On 13 June 2022, Plaintiff and Mr. Stephenson completed a First Report of Injury

Form provided by Defendant-Employer. The answers provided in the “Accident Information &

Incident Facts” section of this form reflect that, at “Lunchtime” on 20 May 2022, Plaintiff

“picked up tool bag wrong = pop!” and that Plaintiff “continued to work not knowing of

damage.”

17.

On 14 June 2022, Plaintiff was evaluated by Dr. Matthew Crawford at

EmergeOrtho. The record from this visit reflects that Plaintiff’s active motion was limited:

“forward flexion 30 degrees, external rotation – 10, abduction 20 degrees.” Dr. Crawford’s note

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 7

further reflects that Plaintiff had “crepitus with forward flexion.” Regarding Plaintiff’s rotator

cuff strength, the note indicated “4/5 subscapularis, 3/5 supraspinatus, 3/5 infraspinatus.” Dr.

Crawford also noted an “external rotation lag sign approximately 40 degrees” and a “[p]ositive

Hornblower’s sign.” The 14 June 2022 note explains that x-rays of Plaintiff’s right shoulder

showed a “medialized glenoid with preserved glenohumeral joint space” as well as “AC joint

arthropathy and type II acromion.” The 14 June 2022 note reflects that Dr. Crawford diagnosed

a “[r]ight rotator cuff tear” and his explanation: “[P]laintiff appears to have a massive rotator

cuff tear based on his significant weakness and inability to perform active shoulder motion

including external rotation lag, inability to forward flex the shoulder and a positive Hornblower’s

sign.” Dr. Crawford ordered an MRI, prescribed Meloxicam, referred Plaintiff to formal

physical therapy, and provided work restrictions of “no lifting, no pushing, [no] pulling, no

overhead use of right upper extremity.” Plaintiff was instructed to return for further evaluation

after the MRI.

18.

Plaintiff never obtained the recommended MRI because his workers’

compensation claim was denied. Furthermore, due to being terminated by Defendant-Employer,

Plaintiff lost his health insurance and could not afford to pay for the scan himself. Plaintiff has

had no further medical treatment for his right shoulder since the 14 June 2022 evaluation by Dr.

Crawford.

19.

On 21 September 2022, Plaintiff, through counsel, filed a Form 18

Notice of

Accident to Employer and Claim of Employee, Representative, or Dependent

which alleges that

on 20 May 2022, Plaintiff sustained injury to his “right shoulder and/or other related injuries”

while “reaching across body in an awkward position with heavy tool bag and shoulder popped.”

On 12 August 2022, Defendants filed a Form 61

Denial of Workers’ Compensation Claim

which

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 8

avers: “[t]here was no injury by accident while in the course of scope of employment.”

20.

After he was terminated by Defendant-Employer, Plaintiff began looking for jobs.

Plaintiff applied to jobs with Fitch Lumber, two Lowes Home Improvement stores, Sherwin

Williams, Town and County Hardware, and Food Lion.

21.

In approximately December 2022, Plaintiff found work as a part-time janitor at a

Food Lion located in Carrboro, North Carolina. Plaintiff testified about the duties he performed

while he worked there:

I came in at seven in the morning, rounded [up] the carts that were

left over from the night before, put them all back in their corral . . .

check[ed] the bathrooms, make sure everything is clean . . . go

through the front where all the cash registers are, clean out all the

trash from there, from behind the cash registers, customer service

area, same thing . . . mopping the floors . . . check for the carts

again, recycle plastic bags previously used from the store.

Plaintiff explained that some of the items he was required to lift he “couldn’t pick up” and that if

he had to lift something heavy, he “could get somebody to help” him because there was “another

guy working there who was doing the same job.” When asked if his right shoulder was a

problem while working for Food Lion, Plaintiff responded: “It was painful, but sweeping a floor

is nothing like picking up a refrigerator.”

22.

Plaintiff testified that he worked “way less than thirty” hours per week at Food

Lion, and that his pay while working at Food Lion “went from $10 to $12 per hour” and that he

initially worked four days per week, but this was subsequently reduced to three days, then two

days, then Plaintiff only worked when there was a need for him. Eventually, he was laid off by

Food Lion.

23.

In total, Plaintiff earned $2,112.27 in wages from Food Lion in 2022. While

working at Food Lion, Plaintiff continued to experience pain and limitations in his right

I.C. NO. 22-030317

Page 9

shoulder.

24.

After his separation from Food Lion, Plaintiff resumed his job search efforts but

was unable to find a job due to his restrictions. Plaintiff testified that he had never had difficulty

finding work prior to his 20 May 2022 injury.

25.

Regarding his present symptoms, Plaintiff testified that his pain has continued.

He explained that it was “[t]hrobbing” and that the pain was currently worse than when he saw

Dr. Crawford. He also related that it felt as if “the muscle[s] are contracted and it’s running all

the way up into my neck and I get numbness in my fingers” and further that the pain keeps him

from sleeping.

26.

Dr. Matthew Crawford, a board-certified orthopedic surgeon who treats shoulder

injuries as a significant part of his practice, was deposed by the parties on 8 August 2023. Dr.

Crawford is the only medical expert who provided testimony in this matter. Dr. Crawford

testified about his “massive rotator cuff tear” diagnosis:

Generally speaking, the term “massive tear” is used if there’s more

than one tendon involved. Based on [Plaintiff’s] exam, lack of

forward flexion, it’s concerning for involvement of the

supraspinatus, which is one of the four tendons. The external

rotation lag is concerning for infraspinatus involvement. That’s a

second tendon. And then the Hornblower’s sign . . . was

concerning for teres minor. So based on my exam, I felt that

potentially three tendons were involved in the injury.

Dr. Crawford testified that, based on Plaintiff’s description of the injury, Plaintiff swinging his

tool bag into the back of the gator on 20 May 2022 more likely than not caused Plaintiff’s rotator

cuff tear.

27.

When informed about the details of the incident during which Plaintiff lifted the

12-pack of beer on 20 May 2022 and when asked if knowledge of that incident changed his

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 10

causation opinion, Dr. Crawford testified:

I think when I'm thinking about mechanism of what could cause a

large rotator cuff injury, it's hard for me to think that lifting a 12-

pack of beer would cause that versus a 60 or 70-pound bag, and the

mechanism of throwing it onto a . . . golf cart or buggy. So I don't

think it really changes my opinion too much.

28.

Dr. Crawford testified that the physical restrictions he put in place following the

14 June 2022 examination, which included no lifting, pushing, pulling, or overhead motion with

his right arm, would still be in place. Dr. Crawford also testified that Plaintiff performing some

work for Food Lion did not change his opinion about Plaintiff’s work restrictions.

29.

The preponderance of the evidence in view of the entire record establishes that, on

20 May 2022, while in the course of his employment with Defendant-Employer, Plaintiff, while

standing on a steep slope, swung his heavy tool bag using only his right arm to place it into a

gator vehicle’s bed. Due to the unusual circumstances present on 20 May 2022, specifically the

gator being parked on a steep slope, this was the only occasion during Plaintiff’s employment

with Defendant-Employer that he performed this task in this manner, and it constituted an

interruption of Plaintiff’s normal work routine and the introduction thereby of unusual conditions

that resulted in Plaintiff’s injury, an event not expected or designed by Plaintiff.

30.

Based upon a preponderance of the evidence in view of the entire record, the Full

Commission finds that Plaintiff has made reasonable but unsuccessful efforts to obtain

employment since being terminated by Defendant-Employer and that, given his age, his previous

work experience in physically strenuous employment, and his lack of education, it would be

futile for him to seek employment within his current medical restrictions. The Full Commission

also finds that Plaintiff’s brief part-time employment with Food Lion does not establish that he is

capable of earning wages in competitive employment, considering that, while working for Food

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 11

Lion, Plaintiff was in pain, was laboring under significant medical limitations, was unable to

perform all of the required duties, was forced to ask for help from coworkers, and has since been

unable to secure other employment.

31.

Based upon a preponderance of the evidence in view of the entire record,

Plaintiff’s medical treatment consequent of his compensable 20 May 2022 injury has been

reasonably necessary to effect a cure, lessen his period of disability, and provide relief.

32.

Based upon a preponderance of the evidence in view of the entire record, Dr.

Matthew Crawford is in the best position to provide Plaintiff’s medical treatment consequent of

the 20 May 2022 injury.

33.

The Deputy Commissioner concluded that Plaintiff, while working for Defendant-

Employer, had an average weekly wage of $802.27, and that this weekly wage yields a weekly

compensation rate of $534.87. Defendants did not appeal these conclusions.

* * * * * * * * * * *

Based upon the foregoing Stipulations and Findings of Fact, the Full Commission makes

the following:

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1.

In workers’ compensation cases, the plaintiff has the burden of proving every

element of compensability. As part of this burden, the plaintiff must present evidence

establishing these elements by a preponderance of the evidence in view of the entire record.

N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-84 (2023);

Harvey v. Raleigh Police Dep’t

., 96 N.C. App. 28, 384. S.E.2d

549,

disc. rev. denied

, 325 N.C. 706, 388 S.E.2d 454 (1989). Regarding the Industrial

Commission’s ability to draw inferences from the evidence presented, the North Carolina Court

of Appeals has held “[it] is for the Commission to determine the credibility of the witnesses, the

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 12

weight to be given the evidence, and the inferences to be drawn from it. . . .”

Rackley v. Coastal

Painting

, 153 N.C. App. 469, 472, 570 S.E.2d 121, 124 (2002).

2.

For Plaintiff’s injury to be compensable under the Workers’ Compensation Act as

an “injury by accident” pursuant to N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-2(6), the injury must be the result of an

“accident” as defined by the Act and case law.

Cody v. Snider Lumber Co

., 328 N.C. 67, 70, 399

S.E.2d 104, 106 (1991). Our courts have explained in detail the requirements of a compensable

“accident” under the Act:

“. . . an unlooked for and untoward event which is not expected or

designed by the person who suffers the injury.” The elements of

an “accident” are the interruption of the routine of work and the

introduction thereby of unusual conditions likely to result in

unexpected consequences. Of course, if the employee is

performing his regular duties in the “usual and customary manner,”

and is injured, there is no “accident” and the injury is not

compensable.

Porter v. Shelby Knit, Inc

., 46 N.C. App. 22, 26, 264 S.E.2d 360, 363 (1980) (internal citations

omitted). Furthermore, it is long held in North Carolina that “the mere fact of injury does not of

itself establish the fact of accident.”

Bigelow v. Tire Sales Co.

, 12 N.C. App. 220, 222, 182 S.E.

2d 856, 858 (1971). The North Carolina Court of Appeals explained this principle within the

context of the requirements of a compensable accident:

[a]n “accident” is not established by the mere fact of injury but is

to be considered as a separate event preceding and causing the

injury. No matter how great the injury, if it is caused by an event

that involves both an employee’s normal work routine and normal

working conditions it will not be considered to have been caused

by accident.

Searsey v. Perry M. Alexander Construction Co.

, 35 N.C. App. 78, 79-80, 239 S.E.2d 847, 849

(1978) (internal citations omitted). In the present case, the unusual circumstances present on 20

May 2020, specifically the gator being parked on a steep slope, led to Plaintiff, for the first time,

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 13

swinging his heavy tool bag into this gator’s bed with one arm, interrupting Plaintiff’s normal

work routine and leading to the unexpected consequence of Plaintiff’s shoulder injury. Given

the foregoing, Plaintiff has met his burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence in

view of the entire record that he sustained a compensable injury by accident arising out of and in

the course of his employment with Defendant-Employer on 20 May 2022. N.C. Gen. Stat. §§

97-2(6), 97-84 (2023);

Porter,

46 N.C. App. At 26, 264 S.E.2d at 363.

3.

Disability is defined by the Act as “incapacity because of injury to earn the wages

which the employee was receiving at the time of injury in the same or other employment.” N.C.

Gen. Stat. § 97-2(9) (2023). The burden is on the plaintiff to prove disability. A plaintiff must

meet this burden by producing evidence that (1) he is incapable after his injury of earning the

same wages he had earned before his injury in the same employment; (2) he is incapable after his

injury of earning the same wages he had earned before his injury in any other employment; and

(3) his incapacity to earn was caused by his injury.

Hilliard v. Apex Cabinet Co

., 305 N.C. 593,

595, 290 S.E.2d 682, 683 (1982).

See

Medlin v. Weaver Cooke Constr., LLC,

367 N.C. 414, 418,

760 S.E.2d 732, 735 (2014). Additionally, the existence and extent of plaintiff’s disability is

established by producing one of the following: (1) medical evidence that he is physically or

mentally, as a result of the work-related injury, incapable of work in any employment; (2)

evidence that he is capable of some work, but that he has, after a reasonable effort, been

unsuccessful in his efforts to obtain employment; (3) evidence that he is capable of some work,

but that it would be futile because of preexisting conditions, such as age, inexperience, or lack of

education, to seek employment; or (4) evidence that he has obtained other employment at wages

less than his pre-injury wages. N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-2(9) (2023);

Hilliard,

305 N.C. at 595, 290

S.E.2d at 683;

Medlin,

367 N.C. at 418, 760 S.E.2d at 735;

Russell v. Lowes Product

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 14

Distribution

, 108 N.C. App. 762, 765, 425 S.E.2d 454, 457 (1993). The Full Commission

concludes that Plaintiff has made reasonable but unsuccessful efforts to obtain employment since

being terminated by Defendant-Employer and that, given his age, his previous work experience

in physically strenuous employment, and his lack of education, it would be futile for him to seek

employment within his current medical restrictions. The Full Commission further concludes that

Plaintiff’s brief part-time employment with Food Lion does not establish that he is capable of

earning wages in competitive employment, considering that, while working for Food Lion,

Plaintiff was in pain, was laboring under significant medical limitations, was unable to perform

all of the required duties, was forced to ask for help from coworkers, and has since been unable

to secure other employment. Plaintiff is therefore entitled to temporary total disability

compensation at the rate of $534.87 per week during this period from 11 June 2022 and

continuing, less the $2,112.27 Plaintiff earned during his employment with Food Lion. N.C.

Gen. Stat. § 97-29 (2023).

4.

Subject to the provisions of N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-25.1, Plaintiff is entitled to have

Defendants provide all medical treatment, incurred or to be incurred, necessitated by the 20 May

2022 compensable accident when bills for the same have been approved pursuant to Industrial

Commission procedures. N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 97-2(19); 97- 25; 97-25.1 (2023). This medical

treatment shall be directed by Dr. Matthew Crawford. N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-25.

* * * * * * * * * * *

Based upon the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, the Full Commission

makes the following:

A W A R D

1.

Subject to a reasonable attorney’s fee herein approved, Defendants shall pay

I.C. NO. 22-030317 Page 15

temporary total disability compensation to Plaintiff at the rate of $534.87 per week for the period

from 11 June 2022 and continuing until Plaintiff returns to work or until further order of the

Commission. The compensation that has accrued shall be paid in a lump sum, less the $2,112.27

Plaintiff earned during his part-time employment with Food Lion.

2.

Subject to the provisions of N.C. Gen. Stat. § 97-25.1, Defendants shall pay all

medical expenses incurred, or to be incurred, as a result of Plaintiff’s compensable right shoulder

condition for so long as such treatment is reasonably necessary to effect a cure, provide relief, or

lessen Plaintiff's period of disability. This medical treatment shall be provided by Dr. Matthew

Crawford.

3.

A reasonable attorney’s fee of twenty-five percent of the compensation due

Plaintiff under paragraph 1 of this Award is approved for Plaintiff’s counsel and shall be paid as

follows: Plaintiff’s counsel shall receive twenty-five percent of the lump sum due Plaintiff, and,

going forward, every fourth compensation check due Plaintiff.

Chair BADDOUR and Commissioner PHILLIPS concur.
